Asian Green Bee-Eater.short_description: A small, slender near-passerine bird with bright emerald-green plumage, black eye stripe, and elongated central tail feathers.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.habitat: Open country, farmlands, dry scrubland, parks, and light woodlands across South Asia.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.geographic_distribution: Widespread across India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and parts of the Middle East.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.diet: Insectivorous, feeding primarily on bees, wasps, dragonflies, and butterflies caught in mid-air.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.identification_features: Bright green body, reddish-orange crown and nape, black gorget collar, yellow-tinted chin, and thin central tail streamers.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.behaviour: Perches conspicuously on telegraph wires or exposed branches, sallying out to capture flying insects before returning to beat them against the perch.
Asian Green Bee-Eater.interesting_facts: Before swallowing bees or wasps, they repeatedly rub the insect against a hard branch to extract the stinger and venom.

Brown-Headed Barbet.short_description: An Asian barbet species characterized by a streak-brown head and neck, bright green body, and heavy orange-red bill.
Brown-Headed Barbet.habitat: Gardens, urban parks, tropical moist forests, and agricultural orchards.
Brown-Headed Barbet.geographic_distribution: Endemic to the Indian subcontinent (India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh).
Brown-Headed Barbet.diet: Frugivorous and insectivorous, consuming wild figs, mangoes, berries, and occasional small insects.
Brown-Headed Barbet.identification_features: Brown streaked head, neck, and breast; bold yellow orbital patch around brown eyes; bright grass-green wings and belly.
Brown-Headed Barbet.behaviour: Arboreal and vocal, renowned for its repetitive, booming 'kutroo... kutroo... kutroo' territorial call during warm summer mornings.
Brown-Headed Barbet.interesting_facts: They excavate nest holes in soft or decaying tree trunks using their powerful, sharp bills.

Cattle Egret.short_description: A cosmopolitan species of heron found in agricultural pastures, marshes, and farmlands.
Cattle Egret.habitat: Pastures, flooded grasslands, agricultural wetlands, and open livestock fields.
Cattle Egret.geographic_distribution: Found globally across Asia, Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Australasia.
Cattle Egret.diet: Carnivorous; feeds on grasshoppers, crickets, frogs, lizards, and small rodents flushed by grazing animals.
Cattle Egret.identification_features: Compact white plumage, yellow bill, greyish-yellow legs. Develops orange-buff plumes on head, neck, and back during breeding season.
Cattle Egret.behaviour: Forms symbiotic relationships with grazing cattle, buffaloes, and tractors, foraging right beside their hooves to catch fleeing insects.
Cattle Egret.interesting_facts: Unlike most herons that wade in deep waters for fish, Cattle Egrets prefer dry land and terrestrial insect foraging.

Common Kingfisher.short_description: A small, brilliantly colored river kingfisher known for high-speed plunge diving for fish.
Common Kingfisher.habitat: Clear streams, rivers, lakes, canals, mangroves, and quiet freshwater bodies.
Common Kingfisher.geographic_distribution: Widespread across Eurasia, North Africa, and the Indian Subcontinent.
Common Kingfisher.diet: Piscivorous; mainly small fish, aquatic insects, freshwater shrimp, and tadpoles.
Common Kingfisher.identification_features: Dazzling iridescent metallic-blue back and wings, rich chestnut/orange underparts, long dagger-like black bill.
Common Kingfisher.behaviour: Perches motionlessly on low branches overhanging water, diving at high velocity to spear fish below the surface.
Common Kingfisher.interesting_facts: Its beak design served as the aerodynamic bio-inspiration for the nose cone of Japan's Shinkansen bullet train.

Common Myna.short_description: A highly adaptable, vocal starling species familiar across urban, suburban, and rural environments.
Common Myna.habitat: Cities, agricultural fields, open country, parks, and roadside human settlements.
Common Myna.geographic_distribution: Native to Asia; introduced globally to Australia, South Africa, and island territories.
Common Myna.diet: Omnivorous; consumes insects, seeds, fruits, human food scraps, and small reptiles.
Common Myna.identification_features: Brown body, black head and neck, bright yellow bill, legs, and bare skin patch behind the eye; prominent white wing patches in flight.
Common Myna.behaviour: Extremely bold and social; frequently walks on the ground and possesses vocal vocalizations and vocal mimicry.
Common Myna.interesting_facts: The Common Myna mates for life and maintains territory year-round with its partner.

Common Rosefinch.short_description: A passerine bird in the finch family, famous for the adult male's deep crimson-rose plumage.
Common Rosefinch.habitat: Thickets, edge of woods, river valleys, shrubby mountain slopes, and overgrown gardens.
Common Rosefinch.geographic_distribution: Breeds across northern Eurasia; winters extensively across India, Nepal, and Southeast Asia.
Common Rosefinch.diet: Granivorous; feeds on seeds, buds, shoots, berries, and occasional small insects.
Common Rosefinch.identification_features: Adult males feature vibrant rose-red head, breast, and rump. Females and young males are streaked olive-brown with pale double wing-bars.
Common Rosefinch.behaviour: Forages quietly in pairs or small flocks among low bushes and seed-bearing weeds.
Common Rosefinch.interesting_facts: The male's melodic song sounds distinctively like 'pleased to meet you'.

Common Tailorbird.short_description: A tiny, active songbird famous for constructing nests by stitching living leaves together.
Common Tailorbird.habitat: Urban gardens, dense scrub, deciduous forests, farmlands, and parks.
Common Tailorbird.geographic_distribution: Native across tropical Asia from India to Southern China and Indonesia.
Common Tailorbird.diet: Insectivorous; preys on tiny beetles, caterpillars, ants, and small spiders.
Common Tailorbird.identification_features: Bright green upperparts, creamy-white underparts, chestnut reddish-brown crown, and long erect cocked tail.
Common Tailorbird.behaviour: Constantly twitches its tail and chirps loudly while flitting rapidly through shrubbery.
Common Tailorbird.interesting_facts: It pierces holes along the edges of broad leaves and sews them together using plant fibers or spider silk to cradle its nest.

Coppersmith Barbet.short_description: A small, colorful barbet famous for its metallic, rhythmic call sounding like a metalsmith striking copper.
Coppersmith Barbet.habitat: Urban gardens, orchards, light woodlands, and wooded parks with fruiting trees.
Coppersmith Barbet.geographic_distribution: Distributed throughout India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia.
Coppersmith Barbet.diet: Frugivorous; prefers wild figs (Ficus species), berries, flower petals, and occasional insects.
Coppersmith Barbet.identification_features: Crimson red forehead and breast patch, yellow eye ring and throat, streak-green belly, and short stubby tail.
Coppersmith Barbet.behaviour: Perches high in tree canopies, calling continuously with a repeated 'tuck... tuck... tuck' sound.
Coppersmith Barbet.interesting_facts: Its rapid territorial tapping call can reach over 108 beats per minute.

Forest Wagtail.short_description: A forest-dwelling passerine bird distinguished by its unique side-to-side tail swaying motion.
Forest Wagtail.habitat: Shady forest understories, bamboo thickets, coffee plantations, and wooded river banks.
Forest Wagtail.geographic_distribution: Breeds in Northeast Asia; winters across Southern India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia.
Forest Wagtail.diet: Insectivorous; hunts ants, beetles, spiders, and earthworms on damp forest floors.
Forest Wagtail.identification_features: Olive-green upperparts, white underparts, bold black double breast-band forming a 'T' shape, and conspicuous white wing bars.
Forest Wagtail.behaviour: Unlike other wagtails that bob their tails vertically, the Forest Wagtail sways its entire rear body horizontally side-to-side.
Forest Wagtail.interesting_facts: It roosts communally in sugarcane fields or reed beds during winter migration.

Gray Wagtail.short_description: A slender wagtail with a remarkably long tail and striking yellow rump and underparts.
Gray Wagtail.habitat: Fast-flowing mountain streams, rocky rivers, waterfalls, and upland canal banks.
Gray Wagtail.geographic_distribution: Widespread across Eurasia; winters in Southern Asia, India, and Africa.
Gray Wagtail.diet: Insectivorous; captures aquatic insects, stoneflies, mayflies, and small crustaceans.
Gray Wagtail.identification_features: Blue-grey upper back, bright yellow belly and vent, dark wings, and exceptionally long black tail with white outer feathers.
Gray Wagtail.behaviour: Constantly bobs its long tail up and down while stepping actively along wet mossy rocks.
Gray Wagtail.interesting_facts: Has the longest tail relative to body length among all wagtail species.

Hoopoe.short_description: A distinctive, cinnamon-colored bird famed for its crown of feathers and black-and-white zebra-striped wings.
Hoopoe.habitat: Open countryside, farmlands, orchards, lawns, and semi-arid grasslands.
Hoopoe.geographic_distribution: Widespread across Europe, Asia, and Africa; resident throughout India.
Hoopoe.diet: Insectivorous; uses its long decurved bill to probe soil for grubs, mole crickets, and pupae.
Hoopoe.identification_features: Cinnamon breast and head, erectile fan-like crest tipped with black, long curved bill, and black-and-white banded wings and tail.
Hoopoe.behaviour: Walks gracefully on lawns, erecting its crest when startled or landing; call is a soft resonant 'oop-oop-oop'.
Hoopoe.interesting_facts: The national bird of Israel and featured prominently in ancient mythology and literature.

House Crow.short_description: A medium-sized, highly intelligent corvid with a slender neck and two-toned grey and black plumage.
House Crow.habitat: Towns, human settlements, cities, markets, and coastal villages.
House Crow.geographic_distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent; introduced to East Africa and parts of the Middle East.
House Crow.diet: Omnivorous scavenger; eats food scraps, insects, small reptiles, eggs, grains, and carrion.
House Crow.identification_features: Glossy black forehead, crown, wings, and tail; contrasting pale grey neck, nape, and upper breast.
House Crow.behaviour: Extremely cunning, adaptable, and social; exhibits advanced problem-solving skills around human habitats.
House Crow.interesting_facts: House Crows are fully dependent on human settlements and rarely survive in pristine uninhabited forests.

Indian Grey Hornbill.short_description: A medium-sized hornbill characterized by grey plumage, long graduated tail, and a black casque on its bill.
Indian Grey Hornbill.habitat: Deciduous forests, urban avenues, botanical gardens, and old fruiting trees.
Indian Grey Hornbill.geographic_distribution: Endemic to the Indian subcontinent (India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Bangladesh).
Indian Grey Hornbill.diet: Frugivorous and carnivorous; eats figs, berries, insects, lizards, and bird eggs.
Indian Grey Hornbill.identification_features: Silvery-grey body, dark grey curved bill with a sharp black casque projecting above it, pale eyebrow, and dark flight feathers.
Indian Grey Hornbill.behaviour: Flies with heavy, undulating flapping followed by glides. Often seen in pairs or small family groups.
Indian Grey Hornbill.interesting_facts: During nesting, the female seals herself inside a tree hollow with mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit for the male to feed her.

Indian Peacock.short_description: The national bird of India, renowned for the male's magnificent iridescent blue neck and train of eyed tail feathers.
Indian Peacock.habitat: Open forest undergrowth, agricultural fields, stream banks, and protected sanctuaries.
Indian Peacock.geographic_distribution: Native to South Asia (India, Sri Lanka, Nepal); introduced globally.
Indian Peacock.diet: Omnivorous; consumes seeds, fallen fruits, insects, small snakes (including vipers), and frogs.
Indian Peacock.identification_features: Males possess metallic blue head and neck, fan crest, and long green tail train with 'eyespots' (ocelli). Females (peahens) are brown and white with green neck patch.
Indian Peacock.behaviour: Roosts high in big trees at night. Males display their upper tail coverts in a massive fan during courtship dances.
Indian Peacock.interesting_facts: The National Bird of India since 1963, celebrated for its snake-hunting ability and spectacular courtship dance before monsoon rains.

Indian Pitta.short_description: A secretive, vibrant ground-dwelling bird nicknamed 'Navrang' (Nine Colors) due to its colorful plumage.
Indian Pitta.habitat: Dense forest undergrowth, evergreen thickets, shaded ravine slopes, and bushy parks.
Indian Pitta.geographic_distribution: Breeds in the Himalayan foothills and Central India; winters in South India and Sri Lanka.
Indian Pitta.diet: Insectivorous; searches leaf litter for beetles, ants, grubs, worms, and snails.
Indian Pitta.identification_features: Green back, blue shoulders, bright yellow belly, bright red vent and under-tail, buff crown with black eye mask.
Indian Pitta.behaviour: Forages quietly on the ground, hopping among dead leaves. Calls around dawn and dusk with a clear double whistle.
Indian Pitta.interesting_facts: In Hindi it is known as 'Navrang' (9 colors), referring to green, blue, yellow, red, buff, black, white, brown, and orange in its feathers.
